section.title: The Broken Covenant
section.sectionRationale: Jeremiah is sent to remind Judah of the covenant sworn at Sinai, obey Me and you will be My people, and to announce that the nation has broken it beyond repair. Their many gods, as numerous as their cities, cannot save them, and the LORD who once called Judah a flourishing olive tree now decrees its branches will be burned.
section.thesis: The covenant Israel swore to keep at the exodus, listen to My voice, has been broken by generations of stubborn disobedience and idolatry, so that the LORD who bound Himself to bless obedience now must bring the covenant curses, yet even this judgment flows from a relationship He initiated and still calls His own.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the terms of the covenant sworn at the exodus and Israel's long history of refusing to obey them; the discovery of a conspiracy of unfaithfulness so deep that God forbids Jeremiah to pray for the people any longer; and the LORD's grieving question over His own beloved house, once a flourishing olive tree, now decreed for burning.

units.label: Listen to the words of this covenant
units.note: cursed is the man who does not obey

verses.text: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD:
“Listen to the words of this {{berith|covenant}} and tell them to the men of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem.
You must tell them that this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: {{arur|Cursed}} is the man who does not obey the words of this covenant,

which I commanded your forefathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace, saying, ‘Obey Me, and do everything I command you, and you will be My people, and I will be your God.’

This was in order to establish the oath I swore to your forefathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as it is to this day.” 
“Amen, LORD,” I answered.
Then the LORD said to me, “Proclaim all these words in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, saying: Hear the words of this covenant and carry them out.
For from the time I brought your fathers out of the land of Egypt until today, I strongly warned them again and again, saying, ‘Obey My voice.’

Yet they would not obey or incline their ears, but each one followed the stubbornness of his evil heart. So I brought on them all the curses of this covenant I had commanded them to follow but they did not keep.”

units.label: There is a conspiracy
units.note: do not pray for this people

verses.text: And the LORD told me, “There is a {{qesher|conspiracy}} among the men of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem.

They have returned to the sins of their forefathers who refused to obey My words. They have followed other gods to serve them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken the covenant I made with their fathers.
Therefore this is what the LORD says: ‘I am about to bring upon them a disaster that they cannot escape. They will cry out to Me, but I will not listen to them.
Then the cities of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem will go and cry out to the gods to which they have been burning incense, but these gods certainly will not save them in their time of disaster.
Your gods are indeed as numerous as your cities, O Judah; the altars of shame you have set up, the altars to burn incense to Baal, are as many as the streets of Jerusalem.’
As for you, do not pray for these people. Do not raise up a cry or a prayer on their behalf, for I will not be listening when they call out to Me in their time of disaster.

units.label: What right has My beloved in My house?
units.note: the olive tree set on fire

verses.text: What right has My beloved in My house, having carried out so many evil schemes? Can consecrated meat avert your doom, so that you can rejoice?
The LORD once called you a flourishing {{zayit|olive tree}}, beautiful with well-formed fruit. But with a mighty roar He will set it on fire, and its branches will be consumed.

The LORD of Hosts, who planted you, has decreed disaster against you on account of the evil that the house of Israel and the house of Judah have brought upon themselves, provoking Me to anger by burning incense to Baal.”

berith.gloss: Covenant, a binding agreement sworn with obligations and sanctions on both sides. This is the same covenant sworn at the exodus, obey Me and you will be My people, now formally charged as broken by Judah's persistent idolatry.

arur.gloss: Cursed, the pronouncement that invokes the covenant's sanctions on one who breaks it. This exact word structures the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy 27 to 28, the legal background this whole oracle assumes.

qesher.gloss: Conspiracy, a binding together for rebellion. God uses the language of political treachery to describe Judah's collective, coordinated turn to other gods, treating covenant unfaithfulness as an act of active betrayal, not passive drift.

zayit.gloss: Olive tree, a symbol of beauty, fruitfulness, and stability in the ancient world. God once called Israel a flourishing olive tree; this same image becomes, in Romans 11, the picture of Israel's branches broken off and Gentile branches grafted in by faith.

basic.context: Jeremiah is commissioned to remind Judah of the covenant terms sworn when God brought their forefathers out of Egypt: obey Me, and you will be My people, and I will be your God. But Judah has repeated the sins of the wilderness generation, chasing other gods until, as the LORD says, there is a conspiracy of unfaithfulness among them. Their many altars to Baal, as numerous as the streets of Jerusalem, cannot save them, and the LORD forbids Jeremiah to intercede any longer.
basic.hermeneutics: This is covenant lawsuit language drawn from Deuteronomy's blessings and curses; Judah is being formally charged with breach of a real, binding relationship, not merely disappointing God in the abstract. The command not to pray for the people, echoed again in chapter 14, is a severe mercy warning of how far things have gone, not a permanent revocation of grace, since this same book later promises restoration.
basic.originalLanguages: The covenant, berith, invoked here is the same word for the Sinai relationship; those who break its terms are arur, cursed, under its sanctions. God names a qesher, conspiracy, among His own people, and mourns that the nation He once called a flourishing zayit, olive tree, now faces the fire.
basic.typology: The flourishing olive tree that Judah once was, now cut down and burned for unfaithfulness, becomes, in Paul's letter to the Romans, the image of Israel's branches broken off and wild branches grafted in by faith, showing that belonging to God's olive tree was always a matter of faithful trust, not mere physical descent.
basic.christ: Jeremiah 31, later in this same book, promises a new covenant to replace the one broken here, a covenant Jesus explicitly inaugurates at the Last Supper, this cup is the new covenant in My blood, Luke 22:20. Where Israel could not keep the covenant's terms and came under its curse, Christ perfectly obeys and becomes cursed in the disobedient's place, Galatians 3:13, so that the olive tree cut down here can, in Him, be grafted and flourish again.
basic.god: God bound Himself to Israel with real, sworn terms; His anger at their unfaithfulness is not arbitrary but the response of a covenant partner betrayed by generations of idolatry. Even His refusal to let Jeremiah intercede reveals how seriously He takes covenant loyalty. Yet the same God who decrees the olive tree's burning is the God who, later in this very book, promises a new and better covenant.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 28 lays out the same covenant blessings and curses invoked here. Romans 11:17-24 develops the olive tree image into Israel and the nations grafted together by faith. Galatians 3:10-13 explains that Christ became a curse for us, the very curse this covenant threatens. Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises the new covenant that answers this broken one.
basic.oneStory: This is the failure of the old covenant under Sinai's terms, a failure so deep God forbids intercession for it, yet the very passage that announces the broken covenant's curse sits inside a book that will later promise a new covenant written on the heart, fulfilled when Christ, cursed in our place, inaugurates that covenant in His own blood.

context.literary:
Jeremiah 11:1 opens a new section with the plain formula, 'the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD,' and the unit runs in three beats that tighten like a legal case. Verses 1 to 8 are the reading of the charter: the terms, the oath, the history of warnings. Verses 9 to 14 are the indictment and the sentence. Verses 15 to 17 are a lament in poetry, a parent's question over a house that has become a stranger to Him. The movement from prose to verse is deliberate. The legal register carries the verdict, and the poem lets us hear what it costs.

The passage is built on repetition. 'Obey' and 'listen' occur in nearly every verse, verses 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10 and 11, and 'this covenant' is named again and again in the first ten verses. A reader cannot miss that the whole issue is hearing. The sentence is a mirror: because they would not listen, God will not listen, verse 11. The verb of the first accusation, 'they would not obey or incline their ears,' verse 8, is the verb God applies to Himself when they cry out.

There is also a quiet circle. The oath that opened the history in verse 5 promised a land flowing with milk and honey, and the poem in verses 16 to 17 ends with the land's own tree burning. And the olive tree, 'planted' by the LORD of Hosts in verse 17, is set beside the idols of verse 13, 'as numerous as your streets,' in a pairing of one planted tree against a forest of altars.

The passage also begins a block, chapters 11 to 20, in which the prophet's biography and his oracles cannot be separated. The first words of that block are not about Jeremiah himself, but at 11:18 the plot against him begins, so that the nation's breach of covenant and the prophet's suffering are placed in the same frame. Those who reject the covenant also reject its messenger.
context.historical:
The covenant that Jeremiah is told to proclaim is the Sinai arrangement as renewed in Deuteronomy. Deuteronomy's shape, with a historical prologue, stipulations, witnesses, blessings and curses, resembles the vassal treaties by which ancient Near Eastern kings bound smaller states to loyalty. In that setting the great King is the LORD, and Israel's vows were the oaths of a subject people. The 'curses' of verse 3 are the formal sanctions that such a treaty named for disobedience, and Deuteronomy 27 and 28 spell them out.

Verses 1 to 8 may reflect the time of Josiah. After the Book of the Law was found in the house of the LORD, 2 Kings 22:8, Josiah gathered the people and 'made a covenant before the LORD to follow the LORD,' 2 Kings 23:3. Jeremiah, who began to prophesy in Josiah's thirteenth year, Jeremiah 1:2, may have been among those sent through 'the cities of Judah' with this word, verse 6. Others place the oracle later, under Jehoiakim, when the covenant renewal had proved to be only a surface change. The text itself says only that the people had gone back to the sins of their forefathers, verse 10, and that Josiah's covenant had not stopped them.

The altars of verse 13 are 'altars of shame,' and the word for shame is bosheth, which was used in Israel as a contemptuous substitute for 'Baal.' The name Esh-baal, 1 Chronicles 8:33, appears as Ish-bosheth in 2 Samuel 2:8 for exactly this reason. Jeremiah's hearers would have caught that the altars are called by the name of the thing they should feel.

The 'consecrated meat' of verse 15 refers to the sacrificial flesh that Judah relied on to keep the covenant secure. Jeremiah has already told them that burnt offerings and meat eaten in the temple do nothing for those who disobey, Jeremiah 6:20 and 7:21-22. The olive was among Israel's most important trees, a source of oil for food, lamps and anointing, so a flourishing olive tree was a natural emblem of blessing, as in Psalm 52:8 and Hosea 14:6.
context.canonical:
The covenant words of verses 3 to 5 gather up lines from across the Torah. 'Cursed is the man who does not obey' repeats the curse formula of Deuteronomy 27:26, and Jeremiah's reply, 'Amen, LORD,' echoes the response the people were told to give at Mount Ebal after each curse, Deuteronomy 27:15-26. 'Obey Me, and ... you will be My people, and I will be your God,' verse 4, combines Exodus 19:5-6 with the covenant formula of Leviticus 26:12. The same formula returns in Jeremiah 7:23, and then, transformed, in the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:33 and in Ezekiel 36:28.

The prophets read the failure as the one the law foresaw. Hosea says Israel, 'like Adam,' transgressed the covenant, Hosea 6:7, and says that the more Israel's fruit increased, the more altars it built, Hosea 10:1, a precise parallel to the altars in verse 13. Jeremiah 31:32 later names this very history: 'a covenant they broke, though I was a husband to them.'

The ban on intercession in verse 14 recalls Moses, who stood in the breach and turned away God's anger at Sinai, Exodus 32:11-14, and Samuel, who said he would not sin by ceasing to pray for the people, 1 Samuel 12:23. In Jeremiah 15:1 God says that even Moses and Samuel could not turn His heart now, and that is how the book measures the depth of Judah's rebellion.

The New Testament takes up the olive tree in Romans 11:16-24, where the root is holy, natural branches have been broken off, and wild branches are grafted in and warned not to boast. It takes up the curse in Galatians 3:10-13. It takes up the covenant in Luke 22:20 and Hebrews 8:6-13, where Jeremiah 31 is quoted at length, and it takes up the burning of useless branches in John 15:6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Jeremiah's task is to convince a people who think they are covenant keepers that they are covenant breakers. They have sacrifices, a temple and a reform behind them. He therefore starts with the terms and not with a general charge. The people agreed to an arrangement, and he reads it back to them. The effect is that the coming disaster stops looking like an accident of politics and starts looking like what their own oath required.

He also wants them to see how old the pattern is. 'From the time I brought your fathers out of the land of Egypt until today,' verse 7, joins Judah to the generation of the exodus. The sin is not a recent decline but a family trait. A people who think they have outgrown the wilderness need to see that they have repeated it.

And he wants them to feel the weight of the divine silence. 'They will cry out to Me, but I will not listen,' verse 11, is no taunt. It teaches that prayer and idolatry cannot be run together, and that crying to Baal and then to the LORD in an emergency does not honour either. The questions in verse 15 are the grieved questions of a father: what is the beloved doing in My house? The prophet is not only a judge, he is also a messenger of heartbreak.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records a verdict on one generation and a command to one prophet. It does not teach that God's silence is the normal condition of any believer who sins, nor that prayer for a failing church or nation is pointless. Paul asks believers to pray for everyone, 1 Timothy 2:1, and Jesus tells His followers to pray for their persecutors, Matthew 5:44. The ban on intercession applies to Jeremiah in a particular season of judgment, and the book repeats it in 7:16 and 14:11 precisely because it is unusual.

What carries forward is the seriousness of covenant. Those who belong to God have been brought out of slavery for a purpose, and a life of religious activity that coexists with other loyalties is an offence to Him, not a lesser form of devotion. The Christian reader also takes the warning of Romans 11:20-22, that the kindness and severity of God belong together, and the promise of Romans 11:23 that those cut off can be grafted in again if they do not persist in unbelief.

debates.question: When was this oracle spoken, and what does Jeremiah's call to 'hear the words of this covenant' refer to?

views.label: Josiah's reform
views.case: Jeremiah was called in Josiah's thirteenth year, Jeremiah 1:2, and the Book of the Law was found in the temple in his eighteenth year, 2 Kings 22:3-8. Verses 1 to 8 read like a preaching tour that supported the covenant renewal of 2 Kings 23:1-3, with Jeremiah crying the words of the covenant in 'the cities of Judah and ... the streets of Jerusalem,' verse 6.

views.label: After Josiah, under Jehoiakim
views.case: Verses 9 to 13 describe a nation that has returned to Baal worship with altars in every street, which sits more easily after the reform has collapsed. On this reading 'this covenant' is the same Deuteronomic covenant, now being used against a people who had made a public show of keeping it.

views.label: A message first given in one period and re-used in another
views.case: Some scholars see the prose as shaped by the book's editors, who gathered Jeremiah's covenant preaching across several reigns. The call to hear and the verdict of broken covenant could both fit more than one date.

debates.bearing: The date changes the story of Jeremiah's early ministry but not the exegesis. In every case the people are charged with breaking a covenant they know, and the verdict is that outward reform is no substitute for obedience.

debates.question: What does the ban on intercession in verse 14 teach about prayer?

views.label: A limited decree about one generation
views.case: It is addressed to Jeremiah alone, the same words appear in 7:16 and 14:11, and 15:1 names Moses and Samuel as intercessors who also would not succeed. The book still goes on to promise restoration, Jeremiah 29:10-14 and 31:31-34, so the ban concerns this judgment, not God's permanent posture.

views.label: A pastoral warning about a point of no return
views.case: Some read it as showing that persistent rebellion can reach a moment when God will no longer hold back the verdict, as in Genesis 6:3 and Hebrews 6:4-6. Intercession remains good for people but not for staying a judgment already decreed.

views.label: A rhetorical blow meant to shock
views.case: Others hold that the command is primarily meant to wake the hearers. The fact that Jeremiah goes on to plead, Jeremiah 14:7-9 and 14:19-22, suggests the ban is intended as a severe instruction that the prophet still wrestles with in prayer.

debates.bearing: The passage guards the weight of sin without closing the door on prayer in general. It also prepares the way for a better Intercessor, Hebrews 7:25, who is never forbidden to plead and never refused.

debates.question: Does the olive tree in verse 16 refer to the nation as a whole or to the covenant community of faith?

views.label: The nation of Israel and Judah as God's planted people
views.case: Verse 17 names 'the house of Israel and the house of Judah' as the ones planted, and the tree is burned for what the house has done. Hosea 14:6 and Psalm 52:8 use the olive as a picture of a flourishing people of God.

views.label: A pattern Paul applies to those who belong by faith
views.case: Romans 11:17-24 takes the olive tree as the people of God from which unbelieving branches are broken and into which believing Gentiles are grafted. The root, the patriarchs and the promise, remains holy, Romans 11:16, so belonging is by faith and not by blood alone.

debates.bearing: The first is the meaning in Jeremiah's day and the second is how the apostles draw out what was always implied: God's planting has never depended on ancestry, and its branches have always been open to trimming and to grafting in.

study.originalLanguages:
The word translated 'obey' in this passage is the Hebrew verb for hearing, shama, and in Jeremiah it governs the whole book. 'Obey My voice' in verse 4 is literally 'hear My voice,' as in Exodus 19:5, and the one who does not 'incline his ear,' verse 8, has refused to bend toward what he has heard. Biblical hearing is a posture of the whole person, which is why the opposite of obeying is not forgetting but hardening. The footnote on verse 7 shows another idiom: God 'earnestly warned them, rising up early and warning them.' The picture is of a master who gets up before dawn to send his message, and Jeremiah uses the same figure of God's persistence elsewhere in the book.

The curse word, arur, is the word on which Deuteronomy 27 hangs its twelve curses, each answered by the people's 'Amen.' It is not a mere insult or the expression of a wish; it names a person set apart from blessing. When Jeremiah answers 'Amen, LORD' in verse 5, he is joining his voice to the oath of the nation.

In verse 8 the phrase 'stubbornness of his evil heart' is Jeremiah's own signature expression. It occurs again in 3:17, 7:24 and 9:14, and has a root in Deuteronomy 29:19, where a man hears the oath and still says he will have peace though he walks in the stubbornness of his own heart. Jeremiah is picking up a phrase from the oath itself.

The 'conspiracy' of verse 9 is qesher, the word for a plot against a king: Absalom's gathering strength, 2 Samuel 15:12, and Athaliah's cry of 'Treason! Treason!' in 2 Kings 11:14. The verb is literally 'found,' so the sense is that a conspiracy has been discovered. Judah's idolatry is treated as treason against the King who made them His people. And in verse 10, the people 'have returned,' using the verb for repentance, shuv, to the sins of their forefathers. Jeremiah's favourite word for turning back to God, as in 3:22, is here used for turning back to the old sins.

The 'altars of shame,' verse 13, use bosheth, shame, the replacement word for Baal. In verse 16 the 'flourishing olive tree' is something God 'planted,' a verb Jeremiah has already used of Israel as a choice vine in 2:21 and which, along with 'uproot,' is part of his commission in 1:10.

Verse 15 is among the harder verses in the book to translate, and the BSB reflects that difficulty with a question that feels broken off: what right has My beloved in My house, and can consecrated meat avert your doom? Readers should hold the details loosely, but the thrust is clear.

typology.type: The olive tree broken and burned, Jeremiah 11:16-17
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah sees a planted tree destroyed for the sin of its branches. Paul takes the olive tree as the people of God, with natural branches broken off for unbelief and wild branches grafted in by faith, Romans 11:17-24. Jesus gives the image its fullest form when He calls Himself the true vine and says that useless branches are gathered and burned, John 15:1-6. The correspondence is that fruitfulness depends on staying joined to the source. The type falls short because Jeremiah's tree is a nation, while Christ is a person in whom both Jew and Gentile are one tree.

typology.type: The curse on the one who does not obey, Jeremiah 11:3
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah repeats the curse formula of Deuteronomy 27:26. Paul takes the same verse and says all who rely on works of the law are under a curse, Galatians 3:10, and then that Christ redeemed us by 'becoming a curse for us,' quoting Deuteronomy 21:23, 'Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree,' Galatians 3:13. The escalation is that the sanction is not escaped but borne. The type falls short in this: the covenant curse fell on the guilty nation, but at the cross it is endured by One who did not break it.

The people were told to say Amen to each curse, Deuteronomy 27:15-26, and Jeremiah says it here. Paul writes that all the promises of God are 'Yes' in Christ, and that through Him our 'Amen' is spoken, 2 Corinthians 1:20, and Revelation 3:14 gives Christ the name 'the Amen, the faithful and true Witness.' Where Israel's Amen to the curse proved unfulfilled in practice, the Son's Amen to the Father's will, even to death on a cross, Philippians 2:8, is complete. The type is an echo and not a prediction, but the title fits.

Moses and Samuel were the great intercessors, and even they would not have turned God's heart in Jeremiah's day, Jeremiah 15:1. Christ is the Intercessor who is never refused: He 'always lives to intercede' for those who draw near, Hebrews 7:25, and is 'at the right hand of God' interceding for us, Romans 8:34. The escalation is that His intercession rests on His own blood. The type falls short in the other direction, since Moses and Samuel pleaded for a people who were still guilty, while Christ's plea is grounded in a sacrifice that has already answered the guilt.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by showing what the old covenant could not do and what it therefore needed. Jeremiah describes the arrangement perfectly: God's promise to be their God, their promise to obey, and a history of failing. In the book's own words a few chapters later the same arrangement is called 'a covenant they broke, though I was a husband to them,' Jeremiah 31:32. God does not drop the pledge; He promises another, one that He writes on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33, and Jesus says over the cup at His last supper, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you,' Luke 22:20. Hebrews 8:6-13 quotes the whole promise and explains that the first covenant was found wanting because the people did not continue in it, and that the new rests on better promises. The very sentence of Jeremiah 11:4, 'you will be My people, and I will be your God,' reappears there word for word.

It leads to Christ by the obedience He supplies. The covenant said, 'Obey My voice,' and God's own verdict was that the people would not. The Father's voice at Jesus' baptism and on the mountain says, 'This is My beloved Son ... Listen to Him!' Matthew 17:5. Notice that the nation here is called 'My beloved,' verse 15, and is asked what right it has in His house. At the temple Jesus claims the house as 'a house of prayer,' Matthew 21:13, and He is the Beloved who does belong there. He was 'obedient to death, even death on a cross,' Philippians 2:8, and 'learned obedience from what He suffered,' Hebrews 5:8. He keeps the covenant the nation broke.

It leads to Christ by the curse. Verse 3 pronounces the curse of Deuteronomy 27:26 on those who do not obey, and Paul says that all who rely on the works of the law are under that curse but that 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:10-13. The tree that is burned in verse 16 is answered by the tree on which Christ hangs, and by His own saying that branches that do not remain in Him are burned, John 15:6, which He applies to Himself as the vine in whom alone fruit grows.

It leads to Christ by the olive tree. Paul's picture in Romans 11:17-24 takes Jeremiah's image of a flourishing tree burned for unfaithfulness and shows what became of it: some natural branches were broken off, wild shoots were grafted in, and the root is still holy. The Messiah is the one through whom the tree has been re-formed, and the way back for broken branches is not their effort but faith in Him, Romans 11:23.

It also leads to Christ by the failed intercession. Moses could not turn God's heart in Jeremiah's day, but Jesus 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25. This is not a forced allegory; the New Testament authors themselves set the failed mediators beside the perfect one.

A caution: the olive tree and the covenant are in Jeremiah about a real nation and a real violation. The links to Christ run through what the New Testament writers say about them, and they should not be inflated into a hidden Christ in every detail of the oracle.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is that He is a covenant maker who commits Himself in words. 'I will be your God' is not sentiment. He swore an oath to the fathers, verse 5, brought them out of the iron furnace, verse 4, and gave them the land that, in Jeremiah's day, is 'as it is to this day.' The God of this chapter keeps His promises, including the ones that hurt. The curses of verse 8 are as much His word as the blessings, and He carries them out.

He is patient to the point of persistence. The footnote to verse 7 speaks of rising up early to warn, as a master who sends messenger after messenger. 'Again and again' is not a description of a short temper. When Judgment comes it comes after a history of warnings, and the phrase 'from the time I brought your fathers out of the land of Egypt until today' measures many centuries of speaking. That helps hold together two things that are easily set against each other, long suffering and severity. His anger is what long love looks like when it is refused.

He is a God whose hearing is a moral matter. Verse 11 says He will not listen to those who cry to Him after refusing to listen to Him, and verse 12 says the gods they have been appeasing will not save them. The chapter will not let us picture God as a service we call on in distress while we serve other loyalties. Yet this is not a God who cannot hear. Elsewhere He promises to answer a people who 'return,' Jeremiah 3:22 and 29:12-13. His silence is a sentence, not a limitation.

He is jealous in the sense that matters. A covenant of marriage, as Jeremiah 31:32 describes it, cannot be shared. The altars 'as numerous as your cities' rival the God who gave the cities. Jealousy here is not insecurity but the claim of a faithful partner on exclusive love.

He is also grieved. The poem of verses 15 to 17 is a question, not a roar: what right has the beloved in My house? A God who had stopped caring would not ask. He once called Judah a flourishing olive tree, 'beautiful with well-formed fruit.' The God who plants is the God who burns, and the same hand does both, verse 17, because He cannot honour both the tree and the treason.

For worship, the passage calls for a hearing that matches His speech. It asks believers to say 'Amen' to His words, including the hard ones, and to treat any religion without obedience, any 'consecrated meat' used as insurance, as the very thing He refuses. And it gives us reason to be grateful that the God who spoke these verses also promised a new covenant in the same book.

crossReferences.note: The twelve curses that Israel affirmed with an 'Amen' on Mount Ebal include the one Jeremiah quotes in 11:3 and the curse on the person who makes an idol, verse 15. Jeremiah's own 'Amen, LORD' in verse 5 places him inside that ceremony and shows he is not inventing a new threat but reading back the one the people swore.

Here the covenant is first offered at Sinai: if the people obey His voice and keep His covenant, they will be His treasured possession, a kingdom of priests. Jeremiah 11:4 compresses this offer into the exodus formula. The comparison shows that the obligation was the condition of the blessing from the beginning.

'I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people.' This is the covenant formula Jeremiah uses in verse 4, taken from the chapter in the law that also lists the sevenfold judgments for breaking it. The same chapter announces blessing and curse, and Jeremiah is applying its second half.

King Josiah gathers the people and makes a covenant before the LORD to keep His commandments with all his heart. This is the most likely background for the public proclamation in Jeremiah 11:6, and it shows how an official covenant renewal could coexist with a heart that had not changed.

'Your gods are as numerous as your cities, O Judah' appears both here and in 11:13. The earlier text asks where the gods are now that trouble has come. Jeremiah 11:12 answers that they will not save, so the two verses together frame the stupidity of a people that multiplies altars and then has nowhere to turn.

Israel was a luxuriant vine, and the more its fruit increased, the more altars it built. Hosea gives the economic side of what Jeremiah describes in verse 13: prosperity led to more shrines, not more gratitude. The comparison shows that blessing, when it is not received as a gift, becomes fuel for idolatry.

God says that even if Moses and Samuel stood before Him, His heart would not go out to this people. It extends the ban of 11:14 and shows what intercession could and could not do. It also sets the greatest earlier intercessors beside Jeremiah, which implies that Jeremiah belongs in their line.

The new covenant is promised to the houses of Israel and Judah, the same two houses named as covenant breakers in 11:10. It is described as unlike the one they broke, with God's law placed in their minds and written on their hearts. This passage is the book's direct answer to the failure of chapter 11.

Paul pictures an olive tree with natural branches broken off and a wild olive shoot grafted in among them. He warns the Gentile believers not to boast, since the root supports them, and says God is able to graft in again those who do not persist in unbelief. This is where Jeremiah's flourishing tree finds its new shape.

Paul quotes the curse of Deuteronomy 27:26 that Jeremiah echoes in 11:3 and says that those who rely on works of the law are under it. Then he says Christ redeemed us by becoming a curse for us. The passage names the way the covenant's penalty was absorbed.

The writer quotes Jeremiah 31 in full and says the new covenant rests on better promises. He notes that the first was found faulty because the people did not continue in it, which echoes the verdict of Jeremiah 11:8-10, and he explains that what is obsolete will soon disappear.

Jesus says He is the true vine, that the Father prunes every branch, and that those who do not remain in Him are thrown into the fire and burned. The picture takes up the vine and olive tree of the prophets and shows that fruit depends on abiding in Him. It answers the burnt branches of Jeremiah 11:16 directly.

study.oneStory:
The covenant of Jeremiah 11 is the second great covenant in the story, and it makes sense only against the first failure. In Eden God placed a man in a garden with a word to keep and a penalty for breaking it, and the man took the fruit, Genesis 2:16-17 and 3:6. Hosea says that Israel, 'like Adam,' transgressed the covenant, Hosea 6:7. The wilderness generation repeated the pattern, the settled nation repeated it again, and Jeremiah's verdict in verses 7 to 10 is that Judah is simply the latest chapter. What the garden showed in one pair, the nation shows in thousands.

God's answer to failure is neither to abandon the plan nor to excuse the sin. He keeps the oath He swore to the fathers, to give them a land, and He keeps it by bringing the curses He promised for disobedience as well as the blessings. Exile, which is what the olive tree's burning means in practice, is the Genesis 3 sentence replayed in history, with another people driven from a land that was a new Eden. Yet even in the sentence there is a promise: the same book that holds these curses announces a covenant that will not be broken, Jeremiah 31:31-34.

The story turns on that promise. Jesus takes the cup and says 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20, and the apostles proclaim that Christ bore the covenant curse on a tree, Galatians 3:13. The nation that could not obey is replaced, in the way that matters, by a Son who did; and those who belong to Him are grafted into the same olive tree, Jew and Gentile together, Romans 11:17-24. Their obedience is no longer the condition but the fruit, since God puts His law within them, Hebrews 8:10.

At the end of the story the words of Jeremiah 11:4 come true without remainder. In the new creation God's dwelling is with humanity, 'they will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God,' Revelation 21:3. The olive tree is replaced by a tree of life on either bank of the river, whose leaves are 'for the healing of the nations,' Revelation 22:2, and the curse is gone, Revelation 22:3. What Judah's altars as numerous as its streets could never provide, the Lamb at the centre of the city does.

sermon.title: Christmas at the Castle, Part 3
sermon.why: Carson reads Jeremiah 11 in full at the start of this message, showing how the covenant curses invoked at Sinai are now falling on Judah for generations of unfaithfulness, precisely the covenant lawsuit this study traces.

quiz.q: What were the original terms of the covenant God reminds Judah of in 11:3-5?

options.text: Obey Me and do everything I command, and you will be My people, and I will be your God.
options.note: Verse 4 states this plainly as the covenant's core term.

options.text: Build a temple in Jerusalem before entering the land.
options.note: Temple building is not the covenant term recalled in this passage.

options.text: Offer burnt offerings every day without exception.
options.note: Sacrifice is not the specific term recalled here; obedience to God's voice is.

options.text: Conquer all the surrounding nations immediately.
options.note: Conquest of Canaan is background history, not the covenant term restated in these verses.

quiz.q: Why does God tell Jeremiah not to pray for the people in 11:14?

options.text: Because their unfaithfulness has gone so far that He will not listen to their cries in the day of disaster.
options.note: Verse 14 states this directly as the reason.

options.text: Because God had already fully forgiven the nation and prayer was unnecessary.
options.note: This is the opposite of what the passage says; judgment, not forgiveness, is being announced.

options.text: Because Jeremiah was too weak or unqualified to intercede effectively.
options.note: The reason given concerns the people's unfaithfulness, not any deficiency in Jeremiah himself.

options.text: Because prayer had been abolished for everyone in Judah from that point on.
options.note: This overstates the command, which is specific to this people's coming disaster, not a general ban on prayer.

quiz.q: How does verse 13 describe the extent of Judah's idolatry?

options.text: They have as many gods as cities, and altars to Baal as many as the streets of Jerusalem.
options.note: Verse 13 states this exact, sweeping comparison.

options.text: They worshiped exactly twelve different gods, one for each tribe.
options.note: This specific number is not stated anywhere in the passage.

options.text: They had remained fully faithful to the LORD alone.
options.note: This directly contradicts the chapter's central charge of widespread idolatry.

options.text: They worshiped only one significant false god, Baal.
options.note: Baal is named, but the text stresses idols as numerous as their cities, not a single false god alone.

quiz.q: What image does God use for Judah in verse 16?

options.text: A flourishing olive tree, beautiful with well-formed fruit, now set on fire.
options.note: Verse 16 uses exactly this image of a once thriving tree now burned.

options.text: A cedar of Lebanon toppled by a storm.
options.note: This is not the specific tree image used in this verse.

options.text: A fortress wall that cannot be breached.
options.note: This image contradicts the passage, which pictures destruction, not impregnable strength.

options.text: A vine trampled underfoot by wild animals.
options.note: Vine and vineyard imagery appears elsewhere in Jeremiah, but the specific image used here is the olive tree.

quiz.q: What can the gods Judah has served do for them in their time of disaster, according to verse 12?

options.text: Nothing at all; they certainly will not save them.
options.note: Verse 12 states this plainly and directly.

options.text: Deliver them fully from the coming disaster.
options.note: This directly contradicts what verse 12 actually says.

options.text: Delay the coming judgment for a limited season.
options.note: No such delay or partial help is described in the text.

options.text: Provide some temporary comfort, though not full deliverance.
options.note: The text states total inability to save, with no mention of even temporary comfort.

questions: God reminds Judah of the covenant's original terms, obey Me and I will be your God. Where in your own walk with God have promises of blessing quietly become detached from a life of obedience?

God tells Jeremiah not to pray for a people so deep in unfaithfulness. Have you ever sensed that persistent, unrepentant sin was hardening a relationship, in your own life or someone else's, past easy intercession?
Judah had as many gods as cities. What competing loyalties or false securities have multiplied quietly in your own life?
God grieves over Judah, once a flourishing olive tree, now set for burning. How does picturing God's grief, and not only His anger, change the way you think about His discipline?
Christ was cursed in the place of those who could not keep the covenant. How does knowing this change the weight you feel over your own past failures to obey?

translationNotes.note: The iron furnace describes the intensity of Egyptian slavery, an image also used in Deuteronomy 4:20, forming the backdrop of the redemption that grounded Israel's covenant obligation.
The altars of shame is a term of deliberate mockery, substituting shame for the honor these altars were supposed to represent.
The olive tree image for Israel recurs in Hosea 14:6 and becomes foundational for Paul's extended argument about Israel and the nations in Romans 11.
